title: Part 1, Chapter 27
paragraphs: How the curate and the barber carried out their plan, together with other matters that deserve a place in this great history

The barber thought the curate’s plan was not just acceptable but so good that they set about putting it into action immediately. They borrowed a petticoat and hood from the innkeeper’s wife, leaving one of the curate’s new cassocks with her as security; and the barber made himself a beard out of a grey-brown — or perhaps reddish — ox-tail, the one the landlord used to keep his comb stuck in. The landlady asked them what they wanted all these things for, and the curate gave her a brief account of Don Quixote’s madness, explaining that the disguise was meant to draw him away from the mountains where he was currently hiding. The landlord and his wife immediately realized that this madman must be their former guest — the man with the balsam, master of the squire who got tossed in the blanket — and they told the curate everything that had happened between him and them, including the part Sancho had kept so quiet about. In the end the landlady dressed the curate up so well that nothing more could be asked: she put him in a cloth petticoat with black velvet stripes a hand’s-width broad, all slashed in the old style, and a bodice of green velvet trimmed with a white satin binding — both the bodice and the petticoat looked as if they dated from the days of King Wamba. The curate refused to let them put the hood on him; instead he wore on his head a little quilted linen cap he normally used as a nightcap, tied a strip of black silk across his forehead, and with another strip made a mask that hid his beard and face very effectively. Then he put on his hat, which was broad enough to double as an umbrella, wrapped himself in his cloak, and seated himself sideways on his mule like a woman, while the barber mounted his own mule wearing a beard that reached down to his waist, a mix of red and white — for it was, as has been said, the tail of a clay-red ox.

They said goodbye to everyone, including the good Maritornes, who — sinner that she was — promised to pray a full rosary so that God would grant them success in the difficult and Christian undertaking they had in hand. But the curate had barely left the inn when it struck him that he was doing something wrong by rigging himself out this way: it was unseemly for a priest to dress like that, even with a great deal at stake. He said as much to the barber and asked him to swap costumes — it was more fitting that the barber play the damsel in distress, while he himself would take the squire’s part, which would be less damaging to his dignity. If the barber refused, he was determined to drop the whole business and let the devil take Don Quixote. Just at that moment Sancho came up, and at the sight of the two of them in such an outfit he could not hold back his laughter. The barber, however, agreed to do what the curate wanted, and with the plan rearranged, the curate began coaching him on how to play his part and what to say to Don Quixote to push and persuade him to come with them and give up his attachment to the spot he had chosen for his pointless penance. The barber said he could manage it perfectly well without any coaching. Since he didn’t care to put the costume on until they were close to where Don Quixote was, he folded up the clothes, the curate adjusted his beard, and they set off with Sancho Panza as their guide. As they went, Sancho told them about their encounter with the madman they had met in the Sierra — though he said nothing about finding the valise and what was inside it; for all his simplicity, the fellow had a streak of greed in him.

The next day they reached the spot where Sancho had laid down broom branches as markers to help him find the place where he had left his master. Recognizing it, he told them this was the way in, and that they had better get into their costumes if that was what it took to rescue his master — for they had already explained to him that going in this disguise and dressing this way was of the highest importance for pulling his master out of the destructive life he had chosen. They gave him strict instructions not to tell his master who they were or admit that he knew them; and if Don Quixote asked — as he certainly would — whether he had delivered the letter to Dulcinea, he was to say yes, and that since she could not read, she had answered by word of mouth, commanding him on pain of her displeasure to come and see her at once. This mattered greatly for Don Quixote himself, they said, because with this story and what they planned to say to him, they were confident of bringing him back to a better way of life and getting him to take immediate steps toward becoming an emperor or a monarch — there was no danger of his becoming an archbishop. Sancho listened to all of it, fixed it firmly in his memory, and thanked them warmly for planning to recommend his master for emperor rather than archbishop, since he felt sure that when it came to handing out rewards to their squires, emperors could do far more than archbishops-errant. He added that it might be a good idea for him to go ahead of them to find his master and deliver his lady’s answer; that alone might be enough to bring him out of the place without putting them to all this trouble. They liked Sancho’s suggestion and decided to wait for him until he came back with word that he had found his master.

Sancho pushed on into the ravines of the Sierra, leaving the two of them in one where a small, gentle stream flowed and where the rocks and trees offered a cool, welcome shade. It was an August day with all the heat of one — and the heat in those parts is intense — and the hour was three in the afternoon, all of which made the spot more inviting and tempted them to wait there for Sancho’s return, which is what they did. They were resting in the shade, then, when a voice reached their ears — unaccompanied by any instrument, but sweet and pleasing in its tone — and it astonished them more than a little, since the place hardly seemed the sort where anyone would sing so well. People often say that woods and fields are home to shepherds with wonderful voices, but that is more poetic fancy than truth. They were even more surprised when they realized that what they were hearing was not the verse of rustic shepherds but the work of polished city wits. And so it proved, for these were the verses they heard:

What makes my search for happiness seem vain? Disdain. What tells me to abandon hope of ease? Jealousies. What holds my heart in an agony of suspense? Absence. If that is so, then for my grief where can I turn to find relief, when hope on every side lies slain by Absence, Jealousies, Disdain?

What proves to be the prime cause of all my woe? Love. What looks with envy on my every chance at glory? Chance. Who gave permission for me to be afflicted so? Heaven. If that is so, I only wait for the blow of an unstoppable fate, since, working for my ruin, these three — Love, Chance, and Heaven — stand in league, I see.

What must I do to find a remedy? Die. What is the cure for love grown cold and strange? Change. What, if all else fails, will heal the heart of sadness? Madness. If that is so, it is pure folly to seek a cure for melancholy: ask where the cure lies, and the answer says in Change, in Madness, or in Death.

The hour, the summer season, the lonely spot, the voice and skill of the singer — everything combined to fill the two listeners with wonder and delight, and they stayed quiet, waiting to hear something more. When the silence stretched on for a while, though, they decided to go looking for the musician who sang with such a fine voice. But just as they were about to move, the same voice stopped them in their tracks; it reached their ears once more, this time singing a
A SONNET

Holy Friendship — when you rose to heaven, soaring up to seek your home beyond the sky and take your seat among the saints on high, you chose to leave behind on earth below your likeness, and on it you bestowed your veil, behind which hypocrisy, parading in your shape, at times deceives the eye and makes its vileness shine as bright as virtue. Friendship, come back to us — or force the fraud who wears your livery now to give it back, since by its help sincerity is being murdered. If you will not unmask your counterfeit, this earth will fall prey to strife once more, as it did when primeval discord held its reign.

The song ended with a deep sigh, and again the two listeners waited attentively for the singer to go on. But when they realized that the music had given way to sobs and heartbroken moaning, they decided to find out who this unhappy person could be — someone whose voice was as remarkable as his sighs were pitiful. They had not gone far when, rounding the corner of a rock, they came upon a man whose look and bearing matched exactly the description Sancho had given them when he told the story of Cardenio. The man showed no surprise at seeing them; he stood still with his head sunk on his chest like someone deep in thought, and after one first glance when they suddenly appeared, he did not raise his eyes to look at them again. The curate, who knew of his misfortune and recognized him from the description, was a man with a good way with words; he went up to him and in a few sensible sentences begged and urged him to give up such a miserable existence, before he lost his life out there — which would be the worst misfortune of all. Cardenio at that moment was in his right mind, free of the fits of madness that so often swept him away, and seeing the two of them dressed in a style so unusual among the people who frequented those wilds, he could not help showing some surprise — all the more when he heard them speak of his situation as if it were common knowledge, which is what the curate’s words implied. So he answered them like this:

“I can see plainly, gentlemen, whoever you may be, that Heaven — which takes care to rescue the good, and quite often the wicked too — has sent me, here in this remote place cut off from all human contact, people I do not deserve: people who want to draw me away from this life to somewhere better, and who use many forceful arguments to show me how unreasonably I am behaving by living the way I do. But since they don’t know what I know — that if I escape this misery I will only fall into one still greater — they will probably write me off as weak-minded, or worse, as a man with no reason left at all. And that would be no surprise, because I myself can tell that the memory of my misfortunes hits me with such force, and works so powerfully toward my ruin, that despite myself I sometimes turn into a kind of stone, without feeling or awareness. I know it is true, because people tell me and show me proof of the things I have done while the terrible fit has hold of me; and all I can do then is grieve uselessly over my lot, curse my fate to no purpose, and offer an excuse for my madness by explaining its cause to anyone who cares to hear it — for no reasonable person who learns the cause will wonder at the effects. And if they cannot help me, at least they will not blame me, and the disgust they feel at my wild behavior will turn into pity for my suffering. So, gentlemen, if you have come here with the same purpose that has brought others, then before you go any further with your wise arguments, I beg you to hear the story of my countless misfortunes. Perhaps once you have heard it, you will spare yourselves the trouble of offering consolation for a grief that is beyond all consolation’s reach.”

Since the two of them wanted nothing more than to hear from his own lips the cause of his suffering, they begged him to tell it, promising to do nothing for his relief or comfort that he himself did not want. With that, the unhappy gentleman began his sad story in nearly the same words and the same manner he had used a few days earlier when telling it to Don Quixote and the goatherd — the time when, thanks to Master Elisabad and Don Quixote’s scrupulous insistence on the proprieties of chivalry, the tale was left unfinished, as this history has already recorded. But now, fortunately, the fit of madness held off and let him tell it through to the end. And so, coming to the incident of the note that Don Fernando had found in the volume of “Amadis of Gaul,” Cardenio said he remembered it perfectly, and that it ran like this:
“From Luscinda to Cardenio.”

“Every day I discover qualities in you that oblige and compel me to value you more highly. So if you want to release me from this debt without any cost to my honor, you can easily do it. I have a father who knows you and who loves me dearly; he will never force my inclination, and he will grant whatever it is reasonable for you to ask — if you really value me as you say you do, and as I believe you do.”

“That letter was what moved me, as I told you, to ask for Luscinda as my wife; that letter was what fixed Luscinda in Don Fernando’s mind as one of the most discreet and prudent women of the day; and that letter was what first planted in him the plan to destroy me before my own plan could be carried out. I told Don Fernando that all Luscinda’s father was waiting for was for my father to ask him for her hand — something I didn’t dare suggest to my father, for fear he would refuse. Not because he failed to recognize Luscinda’s rank, goodness, virtue, and beauty — she had qualities that would do honor to any family in Spain — but because I understood that he didn’t want me to marry so soon, not before we saw what the Duke Ricardo would do for me. In short, I told Don Fernando that I couldn’t bring myself to mention it to my father, partly because of that obstacle and partly because of many other vague discouragements I couldn’t quite name — only that I had a feeling that what I longed for was never going to happen. To all this Don Fernando answered that he would take it on himself to speak to my father and persuade him to speak to Luscinda’s. Oh, ambitious Marius! Oh, cruel Catiline! Oh, wicked Sylla! Oh, perfidious Ganelon! Oh, treacherous Vellido! Oh, vindictive Julian! Oh, covetous Judas! Traitor — cruel, vindictive, and perfidious — how had this poor wretch failed in his loyalty to you, when he so openly showed you the secrets and joys of his heart? What offense did I commit? What words did I say, what advice did I give, that wasn’t aimed entirely at advancing your honor and your welfare? But what am I complaining about, miserable as I am? When misfortunes come down from the stars, they descend from such a height and fall on us with such fury and violence that no power on earth can check their course and no human scheme can hold off their coming. Who would have thought that Don Fernando — a highborn gentleman, intelligent, bound to me by gratitude for my services, a man who could win the object of his love wherever he chose to set his affections — would harden himself, as the saying goes, to the point of robbing me of my one ewe lamb, which wasn’t even yet in my possession? But let me set aside these useless, unavailing reflections and pick up the broken thread of my unhappy story.

“To go on, then: Don Fernando found that my presence stood in the way of carrying out his treacherous and wicked design, so he decided to send me to his elder brother on the pretext of asking him for money to pay for six horses. He had bought them deliberately, with the sole aim of getting me out of the way so he could carry out his infernal scheme more easily — he bought them the very day he offered to speak to my father — and now he wanted me to go and fetch the payment. Could I have anticipated this betrayal? Could I possibly have suspected it? Of course not — far from it, I offered with the greatest pleasure to leave at once, delighted at the good bargain that had been struck. That night I spoke with Luscinda and told her what had been agreed with Don Fernando, and how I had strong hopes that our fair and reasonable wishes would come true. She, as unsuspecting of Don Fernando’s treachery as I was, urged me to come back quickly, since she believed the fulfillment of our desires would be delayed only as long as my father put off speaking to hers. I don’t know why, but as she said this her eyes filled with tears and a lump rose in her throat, stopping her from saying a single word of the many more it seemed to me she was trying to say. I was astonished at this strange mood, which I had never seen in her before; whenever luck and my ingenuity gave us the chance, we had always talked with the greatest gaiety and cheerfulness, never mixing tears, sighs, jealousies, doubts, or fears into our words. On my side it was all celebration of my good fortune that Heaven had given her to me as my lady: I glorified her beauty, I extolled her worth and her understanding; and she paid me back by praising in me whatever, loving me as she did, she thought worth praising. Beyond that we had a hundred thousand small things to talk about — the doings of our neighbors and acquaintances — and the boldest thing I ever did was to take, almost by force, one of her lovely white hands and press it to my lips, as far as the narrowness of the low grating between us allowed. But the night before the miserable day of my departure, she wept, she moaned, she sighed, and then she withdrew, leaving me bewildered and shaken, overwhelmed by these strange and painful signs of grief and sorrow in Luscinda. Not wanting to crush my own hopes, I put it all down to the depth of her love for me and the pain that separation causes those who love tenderly. In the end I set off, sad and dejected, my heart full of imaginings and suspicions, without knowing exactly what it was I suspected or imagined — plain omens, pointing to the sad event and the misfortune that lay waiting for me.

“I reached the place I had been sent to and gave the letter to Don Fernando’s brother. I was received kindly, but not dispatched quickly: to my great frustration, he told me to wait eight days, somewhere the duke his father would not be likely to see me, because his brother had written that the money was to be sent without their father’s knowledge. All of this was a scheme of the treacherous Don Fernando, since his brother had no shortage of money and could have sent me off at once.

“It was an order that sorely tempted me to disobey, because it seemed impossible to endure life for so many days separated from Luscinda — especially after leaving her in the sorrowful state I have described to you. Even so, like a dutiful servant, I obeyed, though I felt it would come at the cost of my well-being. But four days later a man arrived looking for me, carrying a letter; from the address I could see it came from Luscinda, for the handwriting was hers. I opened it in fear and trembling, convinced that only something serious would have driven her to write to me at a distance, since she rarely did so even when I was near. Before reading it, I asked the man who had given it to him and how long he had been on the road. He told me that he happened to be passing through one of the city’s streets around noon when a very beautiful lady called to him from a window. With tears in her eyes, she said to him hurriedly, ‘Brother, if you are a Christian, as you seem to be, I beg you for the love of God to have this letter sent without a moment’s delay to the place and the person named on the address — both are well known — and in doing this you will do a great service to our Lord. And so that you are at no inconvenience in doing it, take what is in this handkerchief.’ ‘And with that,’ he said, ‘she threw a handkerchief out of the window with a hundred reals tied up in it, along with this gold ring I have brought here together with the letter I have given you. Then, without waiting for any answer, she left the window — though not before she saw me take the letter and the handkerchief and signal to her that I would do what she asked. Seeing myself so well paid for the trouble of bringing it to you, and knowing from the address that it was meant for you — because, señor, I know you very well — and unable, besides, to resist that beautiful lady’s tears, I decided to trust no one else but to come and deliver it to you myself. And in the sixteen hours since it was handed to me, I have made the journey, which, as you know, is eighteen leagues.’

“The whole time this kind-hearted improvised courier was telling me this, I hung on his words, my legs trembling beneath me so badly I could barely stand. At last I opened the letter and read these words:

Don Fernando has kept the promise he gave you to urge your father to speak to mine — but he has kept it in a way that serves him far more than it helps you. I must tell you, señor, that he has asked for my hand, and my father, swayed by what he sees as Don Fernando’s superiority over you, has welcomed his suit so warmly that the betrothal is set to take place two days from now, in such secrecy and so privately that the only witnesses will be the Heavens above and a few members of the household. Imagine the state I am in; decide for yourself whether it is urgent for you to come; whether I love you or not, the outcome of this affair will show you. God grant that this reaches your hand before mine is forced to join itself with the hand of a man who keeps his pledged word so badly.

“Those, in brief, were the words of the letter — words that made me set out at once without waiting any longer for the reply or the money, for I now saw clearly that it was not the purchase of horses but the pursuit of his own pleasure that had made Don Fernando send me to his brother. My fury at Don Fernando, combined with the fear of losing the prize I had won through so many years of love and devotion, gave me wings: almost flying, I reached home that same day, at the hour that served for speaking with Luscinda. I arrived unseen, left the mule I had ridden at the house of the good man who had brought me the letter, and fortune was kind enough, for once, that I found Luscinda at the grating that had been the witness of our love. She recognized me at once, and I her — but not as she should have recognized me, nor I her. But who in this world can claim to have fathomed or understood the wavering mind and unstable nature of a woman? No one, truly. To continue: the moment Luscinda saw me, she said, ‘Cardenio, I am in my wedding dress. The treacherous Don Fernando and my greedy father are waiting for me in the hall, with the other witnesses — who will witness my death before they witness my betrothal. Don’t be distressed, my friend, but find a way to be present at this sacrifice. If my words cannot prevent it, I have a dagger hidden on me that can prevent more deliberate violence, by ending my life and giving you a first proof of the love I have borne you and bear you still.’ I answered her distractedly and in haste, terrified I would not have time to answer at all: ‘May your deeds make good your words, my lady. If you carry a dagger to save your honor, I carry a sword to defend you — or to kill myself, if fortune turns against us.’

“I don’t think she could have heard all of those words, because I saw them calling her away in a hurry — the bridegroom was waiting. Then the night of my sorrow closed in; the sun of my happiness set; my eyes were left without sight, my mind without reason. I could not bring myself to enter the house; I was incapable of any movement at all. But reflecting on how important it was that I be present for whatever might happen, I steadied myself as best I could and went in — I knew all the entrances and exits well, and besides, with the secret commotion running through the house, no one noticed me. Without being seen, I managed to station myself in the recess formed by a window of the hall itself, hidden by the ends and borders of two tapestries, from between which I could watch everything that happened in the room without being observed. Who could describe the agitation of heart I suffered as I stood there — the thoughts that came to me, the reflections that ran through my mind? They were such as cannot be told, and perhaps should not be. Let it be enough to say that the bridegroom entered the hall in his everyday clothes, without ornament of any kind. As groomsman he had with him a cousin of Luscinda’s, and apart from the household servants there was no one else in the room. A little later, Luscinda came out from an antechamber, accompanied by her mother and two of her maids, dressed and adorned as suited her rank and beauty, in full festival and ceremonial attire. My anxiety and distraction didn’t let me observe or note the details of what she wore; I could only take in the colors — crimson and white — and the glitter of the gems and jewels on her headdress and clothing, all of it outshone by the rare beauty of her lovely auburn hair, which rivaled the precious stones and the light of the four torches standing in the hall, and gleamed brighter than them all. Oh memory, mortal enemy of my peace! Why set before me now the incomparable beauty of that adored enemy of mine? Wouldn’t it be better, cruel memory, to remind me and replay what she did then, so that, stirred by so glaring a wrong, I might seek — if not vengeance now — at least an end to my own life? Don’t grow tired, gentlemen, of listening to these digressions. My sorrow is not the kind that can or should be told tersely and briefly; to me, every part of it seems to demand many words.”

To this the curate replied that far from being tired of listening to him, they found the details he mentioned deeply interesting — they were the kind of thing that should by no means be left out, and they deserved the same attention as the main story.

“To continue, then,” Cardenio went on: “when everyone was assembled in the hall, the parish priest came in, and as he took the couple by the hand to perform the required ceremony, he spoke the words, ‘Will you, Señora Luscinda, take Señor Don Fernando, here present, as your lawful husband, as holy Mother Church ordains?’ At that I thrust my head and neck out from between the tapestries and, with straining ears and a pounding heart, set myself to listen for Luscinda’s answer — waiting on her reply for my death sentence or the granting of my life. Oh, if only I had dared at that moment to rush forward and shout, ‘Luscinda, Luscinda! Watch what you are doing; remember what you owe me; remember that you are mine and cannot belong to another; understand that the instant you say “Yes” is the instant my life ends! Oh, treacherous Don Fernando — thief of my glory, death of my life! What do you want? Realize that as a Christian you cannot achieve what you desire, for Luscinda is my bride, and I am her husband!’ Fool that I am — now that I am far away and out of danger, I say I should have done what I did not do; now that I have let my precious treasure be stolen from me, I curse the thief, on whom I might have taken vengeance if I had as much heart for that as I have for lamenting my fate. In short, since I was a coward and a fool then, it is no great wonder that I am dying now — ashamed, remorseful, and mad.

“The priest stood waiting for Luscinda’s answer, and for a long while she withheld it. Just when I thought she was about to draw the dagger to save her honor, or to find the words for some declaration of the truth that would speak on my behalf, I heard her say in a faint, feeble voice, ‘I will.’ Don Fernando said the same; he gave her the ring, and they stood bound by a knot that could never be undone. The bridegroom then stepped forward to embrace his bride, and she, pressing her hand against her heart, fell fainting into her mother’s arms. It only remains now to tell you the state I was in when, in that consent I had just heard, I saw all my hopes mocked, Luscinda’s words and promises exposed as lies, and the recovery of the prize I had lost in that instant made impossible forever. I stood there stunned, abandoned — it seemed — by Heaven itself, declared an enemy by the very earth that bore me, the air refusing me breath for my sighs, the water refusing moisture for my tears; only fire gathered strength, until my whole body burned with rage and jealousy. The whole company was thrown into confusion by Luscinda’s fainting, and as her mother loosened her dress to give her air, a sealed paper was discovered in her bosom. Don Fernando seized it at once and began to read it by the light of one of the torches; and when he had finished, he sat down in a chair, resting his cheek on his hand like a man deep in thought, taking no part in the efforts being made to revive his bride from her faint.

“Seeing the whole household in confusion, I risked coming out, indifferent to whether I was seen or not — and determined, if I was seen, to do something so frenzied that the whole world would understand the righteous indignation in my breast, through the punishment of the treacherous Don Fernando and even of that fickle, fainting traitress. But my fate, no doubt holding me in reserve for greater sorrows — if greater ones exist — arranged things so that at that moment I had an abundance, even a surplus, of the very reason that has failed me ever since. And so, instead of taking revenge on my worst enemies (which would have been easy, since no one’s thoughts were anywhere near me), I resolved to take it on myself instead — to inflict on myself the pain they deserved, perhaps with even greater severity than I would have shown them if I had killed them on the spot; for sudden pain is quickly over, but pain drawn out by torment kills continually without ever ending a life. In short, I left the house and went to the house of the man with whom I had left my mule. I had him saddle it for me, mounted without a word of farewell, and rode out of the city like another Lot, not daring to turn my head to look back at it. When I found myself alone in the open country, screened by the darkness of the night and tempted by the stillness to pour out my grief without worry or fear of being heard or seen, I broke my silence and raised my voice in curses against Luscinda and Don Fernando, as if cursing could avenge the wrong they had done me. I called her cruel, ungrateful, false, and thankless — but above all greedy, since my enemy’s wealth had blinded the eyes of her love and turned it away from me, handing it over to a man on whom fortune had been more generous and openhanded. And yet, in the middle of this storm of curses and reproaches, I found excuses for her. It was no wonder, I said, that a young girl, sheltered in her parents’ house, raised and trained to obey them always, should have been ready to bow to their wishes when they offered her as a husband a gentleman of such distinction, wealth, and noble birth; if she had refused him, people would have thought she was out of her mind, or that her affections were set elsewhere — a suspicion damaging to her good name and reputation. But then again, I said, if she had declared that I was her husband, they would have seen that in choosing me she had not chosen so badly that they couldn’t forgive her; for before Don Fernando made his offer, her parents themselves — if their wishes had been governed by reason — could not have wanted a more suitable husband for their daughter than I was. And she, before taking the final, fatal step of giving her hand, could easily have said that I had already given her mine, and I would have come forward to back up any such claim she made. In the end I concluded that weak love, too little reflection, great ambition, and a craving for rank had made her forget the words with which she had deceived me — words I had trusted, sustained by my firm hopes and my honorable passion.

“Talking to myself this way, in turmoil, I traveled on through the rest of the night, and at daybreak I reached one of the passes into these mountains. I wandered through them for three more days, following no path or road, until I came to some meadows lying on I don’t know which side of the range, and there I asked some herdsmen where the most rugged part of these mountains lay. They told me it was in this direction, and I headed here at once, intending to end my life in this place. But as I was picking my way among these crags, my mule dropped dead from exhaustion and hunger — or, as I think more likely, simply to be rid of the worthless burden it carried in me. I was left on foot, worn out and starving, with no one to help me and no thought of looking for help. I lay stretched out on the ground for I don’t know how long, and when I got up my hunger was gone, and I found some goatherds beside me — no doubt the people who had relieved my need, because they told me how they had found me, and how I had been raving in a way that made it plain I had lost my reason. Since then, I have been aware that I am not always in full possession of it: at times I am so deranged and crazed that I do a thousand mad things — tearing my clothes, crying aloud through these solitudes, cursing my fate, and calling pointlessly on the dear name of the woman who is my enemy, with no aim in those moments but to end my life in lamentation. And when I come back to my senses, I find myself so drained and weary that I can barely move. Most often my dwelling is the hollow of a cork tree, big enough to shelter this miserable body. The herdsmen and goatherds who pass through these mountains, moved by compassion, supply me with food, leaving it by the wayside or on the rocks where they think I might pass by and find it; and so, even when I am out of my senses, the needs of nature teach me what is required to keep me alive, and make me crave it and reach for it. At other times — so they tell me, when they find me in a rational state — I come out onto the road and snatch food by force from the shepherds carrying it from the village to their huts, even though they would gladly give it to me. This is how I pass the wretched remainder of my life, until Heaven wills it to end, or wills my memory so reordered that I no longer remember Luscinda’s beauty and treachery or the wrong Don Fernando did me. If Heaven will do that without taking my life, I will turn my thoughts to some better course; if not, I can only pray it to have full mercy on my soul, for I feel no power or strength in myself to free my body from this hardship into which I have chosen, of my own accord, to place it.

“That, gentlemen, is the bitter story of my misfortune. Tell me whether it could be told with less emotion than you have seen in me — and don’t trouble yourselves with urging or pressing on me whatever reason suggests might serve for my relief, for it will do me as much good as a wise physician’s prescription does the sick man who refuses to take it. I want no health without Luscinda; and since it is her pleasure to belong to another, when she is mine — or should be — let it be my pleasure to belong to misery when I might have enjoyed happiness. By her fickleness she tried to make my ruin permanent; I will try to satisfy her wishes by pursuing my own destruction. And future generations will see that I alone lacked the thing every other unfortunate has in abundance: for them, the impossibility of consolation is itself a consolation, while for me it is the cause of greater griefs and sufferings, because I believe they will not end even in death.”

Here Cardenio brought his long discourse and story to a close — a tale as full of misfortune as it was of love. But just as the curate was about to offer him some words of comfort, he was stopped by a voice that reached his ear, saying in mournful tones what will be told in the Fourth Part of this narrative; for at this point the wise and shrewd historian, Cid Hamete Benengeli, brought the Third Part to its conclusion.
